header.summary: Name winegcc's temp directory deterministically, for reproducible builds
header.upstream:
candidate (draft in .local/bug-reports/; it only changes
winegcc's temp directory name)
header.why:
winegcc links each PE file from a spec object in a temp directory named
after the time and pid (tools.h make_temp_dir). lld-link records that path in
the PDB, and the PDB's hash becomes the PE file's debug GUID and, with
-Brepro, its timestamp. So every PE file differed between two otherwise
identical builds. Naming the directory after a hash of the command line makes
the path, and so the files, the same each time. compile.sh sets TMPDIR to a
fixed path, so it doesn't depend on the build machine's user either.
The hash leaves out winegcc's own path (in the build directory) and the
--cc-cmd/--ld-cmd values (a compiler cache's wrapper instead of the
compiler), which differ between builds that should match: with them in,
builds with and without ccache differed in every PE file.
It doesn't change what Wine does at run time.

header.summary: Build the dwrite tests with -fno-builtin so they link with LLVM 23
header.upstream:
differently (9195d892, Wine 10.12: configure builds every PE file
with -ffp-exception-behavior=maytrap, which stops the rewrite)
header.why:
LLVM 23 (our llvm-mingw, clang 23.1.4) turns floor() of a value it
knows is not negative into trunc() when floating-point exceptions may be
ignored. The dwrite tests import msvcrt, whose import library has no trunc
or truncf (Windows' msvcrt.dll doesn't export them), so dwrite_test.exe
failed to link on Wine 10.0: "undefined symbol: trunc". -fno-builtin stops
the compiler treating floor() as something it can rewrite, as Wine already
does for its own CRT (MSVCRTFLAGS). Only for layout.c, where floor() is used:
EXTRADEFS also goes to wrc, which rejects the option. Wine 10.12 and later
build every PE file with -ffp-exception-behavior=maytrap, which keeps the
call as floor() (measured with this compiler on layout.c of 10.0, 11.21
and 11.22), so they don't need it.
It changes only dwrite_test.exe (in the -tests release file).

header.summary: Wait longer for the Cocoa app to start on a busy Mac, and don't crash when the wait runs out
header.upstream:
candidate (draft in .local/bug-reports/). The bug is in WineHQ
10.0 to master (2026-11-25) and in CrossOver 26.3.0.
header.why:
macdrv_start_cocoa_app waits 5 s for the main thread to turn into a
Cocoa app. On a Mac with every core busy, under Rosetta, that can be
missed: the process then has no display driver ("Failed to start Cocoa app
main loop"). Worse, the startup info was on the waiting thread's stack and
the run-loop source was only released, never invalidated, so when the main
thread got to it later it read a dead frame and crashed. Now the info is on
the heap, counted (the source holds a reference), the source is
invalidated on timeout, and the wait is 60 s by default, set by
CocoaStartTimeout (a string, seconds, 1-3600) under
HKCU\Software\Wine\Mac Driver (or the per-app key). Processes with no
graphics session are still refused earlier, in macdrv_init, so SSH runs
fail as fast as before.

Cocoa app. On a Mac with every core busy, under Rosetta, that can be
missed: the process then has no display driver ("Failed to start Cocoa app
main loop"). Worse, the startup info was on the waiting thread's stack and
the run-loop source was only released, never invalidated, so when the main
thread got to it later it read a dead frame and crashed. Now the info is on
the heap, counted (the source holds a reference), the source is
invalidated on timeout, and the wait is 60 s by default, set by
CocoaStartTimeout (a string, seconds, 1-3600) under
HKCU\Software\Wine\Mac Driver (or the per-app key). Processes with no
graphics session are still refused earlier, in macdrv_init, so SSH runs
fail as fast as before.

header.summary: Don't deadlock when a window's OpenGL context is updated from the main thread
header.uncertain:
how the main thread reached this branch: a pending context
normally still has its latent view. Most likely a GL thread consumed it at

header.upstream:

header.why:
macdrv_update_opengl_context updates the context through
OnMainThread, which queues the block on the main thread's run loop and
waits for it. OnMainThread doesn't check whether it's already on the main
thread, and the content view's viewWillDraw calls

in wglSwapBuffers, for one). Update the context directly when already on
the main thread, as the function's other branches already do.

viewWillDraw -> macdrv_update_opengl_context -> OnMainThread, entered from

header.summary: Don't release a freed OpenGL context on the main thread after it's deallocated on a GL thread
header.upstream:
candidate (draft in .local/bug-reports/). The code is the same
in WineHQ 10.0 to master and in CrossOver 26.3.0 (checked 2026-11-25).
header.why:
-[NSOpenGLContext dealloc] always calls -clearDrawable, which
WineOpenGLContext overrides. Off the main thread the override runs [super
clearDrawable] in a block sent to the main thread with OnMainThread, and
the block retains self. When a GL thread drops the last reference (the
context is usually freed on the main thread instead, when the block that
removes it from its view is released), that happens during dealloc: the
main thread runs the block, OnMainThread returns, the GL thread finishes
freeing the context, and the main thread then releases the block and with
it the freed context. objc_release reads freed memory and the process dies
("Exception c0000005 in system thread", at objc_release+34). The block now
holds an unretained reference: OnMainThread waits for the block to run, so
the context outlives its use.
Also, -dealloc released the view and then [super dealloc] called
-clearDrawable, which released it again whenever the context still had a
view. -dealloc now clears the drawable first, so the view is released
once.
Native stacks of three caught crashes all ended in objc_release from this
block's dispose helper, released on the main thread. A native probe
(macOS 26) shows -[NSOpenGLContext dealloc] calling -clearDrawable with and
without a view, and [super clearDrawable] neither retaining nor
autoreleasing the context.
Upstream winemac has the same code in 10.0; why 11.x shows the crash more
often isn't known (Wine 11's wined3d may release contexts on its command
thread, which has no event queue).

header.summary: Report the user's registers for a thread suspended on its way out of a syscall
header.uncertain:
Linux has the same window (frame+0x70 before iretq) without the
extra system call, so there it should be rare; not tested there. The
window is small enough on 10.0 that a run of the test could see no
context in it.
header.why:
SuspendThread reaches the thread as SIGUSR1, and usr1_handler saves
the context that GetThreadContext later returns. If the thread is in a
syscall it saves the user's registers from the syscall frame; otherwise it
takes the signal context as user code. It decides with is_inside_syscall,
which only covers the kernel stack up to the frame. On its way out of a
syscall, though, __wine_syscall_dispatcher points rsp into the frame
(frame+0x70, to load the user's rsp or for iretq). A suspend landing
there saved the dispatcher's own registers as the thread's context: rsp
on Wine's kernel stack, just below the thread's stack, and rip in the
dispatcher. Now a thread whose sp is in the frame is treated as in the
syscall too: its context is built below the frame, not over it. (On 11.x
the dispatcher also restores the user's gs base from there, and the 11.x
copy runs leave_handler afterwards; 10.0's dispatcher keeps gs on the TEB
on macOS.) Other users of is_inside_syscall are unchanged. On 10.0 the
window is only a few instructions: tests/regress/suspend-context-syscall-return
saw 838 of 159544 contexts with rsp outside the stack on
macfixes-10.0-build7.

header.summary: Wait up to 120 s, not 10 s, for explorer to set up the desktop
header.upstream:
candidate (draft in .local/bug-reports/). WineHQ master still
waits 10 s (checked 2026-11-25); so does CrossOver 26.3.0.
header.why:
The first process of a session to need the desktop starts
explorer.exe /desktop and waits for it to go idle, which it does once it
has loaded the display driver, created the desktop window and registered
the display devices. The wait gave up after 10 s. The process then had the
server create a bare desktop window, which has no display-device GUID, so
load_desktop_driver found no GraphicsDriver and the process stayed on the
null driver for the rest of its life ("The explorer process failed to
start.", nodrv_CreateWindow): no windows, no Direct3D device. With every
core busy under Rosetta, explorer can take far longer than 10 s; its own
Mac driver may wait up to 60 s for Cocoa (winemac-cocoa-start-wait). The
wait is now 120 s; it still ends at once if explorer exits.
With explorer made 15 s late (a graphics driver listed before the Mac
driver that sleeps 15 s and fails), a program's CreateWindowEx failed
after 10.1 s on 11.22, and got its window after 17 to 18 s with this
change.

session). Client surfaces made per get_win_data call stay in the window's

build doesn't support D3DMetal on Wine 11.x.

header.why:
DXMT's d3d11.dll and dxgi.dll import winemetal.dll, which DXMT ships

build0). Building a stub winemetal.dll makes wineboot put one in system32
and syswow64; with DXMT's on the DLL path, loading the name loads DXMT's.
Without DXMT, the stub loads and exports only WineMetalEntry.

header.summary: Add a winemetal.dll stub so DXMT's DLLs can load
header.why:
DXMT's d3d11.dll and dxgi.dll import winemetal.dll, which DXMT ships
(PE and Unix parts) on its DLL path (WINEDLLPATH_DXMT). Outside prefix
setup, Wine loads a builtin DLL only if a file of that name is in the
prefix (find_builtin_without_file in dlls/ntdll/loader.c), so without one
DXMT's winemetal.dll and d3d11.dll fail with error 126 (shown on 10.0
build0). Building a stub winemetal.dll makes wineboot put one in system32
and syswow64; with DXMT's on the DLL path, loading the name loads DXMT's.
Without DXMT, the stub loads and exports only WineMetalEntry.

macOS only offers forward-compatible 3.2+ core contexts, and Wine 10.0's
Mac driver refuses a 3.2-4.1 context request without

the program is that deprecated features (wide lines) are unavailable,
which a core context mostly lacks anyway. Wine 11 behaves this way without
being asked, so the 11.x builds don't need the patch.

header.programs:
Second Chance (an app that embeds Wine): had to patch a load
command into winemac.so and re-sign it to load its in-process helpers
header.related_note:
they also
change setup_options and macdrv_init
header.risk:
loads native code (dlopen, RTLD_NOW | RTLD_GLOBAL) into every Wine
process that starts the Mac driver, from the paths in WINEMAC_PLUGINS.
Whoever sets the environment Wine starts in turns it on, and child
processes inherit it. Unsigned plugins load (Wine isn't hardened-runtime).
header.summary: winemac: load plugin libraries named in WINEMAC_PLUGINS before Cocoa starts
header.uncertain:
a plugin that needs to run before the Mac Driver options are
read, or after Cocoa has started, isn't served by this point; none known.
header.why:
An app that embeds Wine may need code of its own inside the Mac driver
(Objective-C hooks on Wine's windows, say). Without a hook it has to add a
load command to winemac.so and re-sign it. Now macdrv_init dlopens each
path in the WINEMAC_PLUGINS environment variable (a colon-separated list,
inherited by child processes), after reading the options and before Cocoa
starts. Only absolute paths are loaded: a path that doesn't start with /,
or doesn't load, is logged (err:macdrv) and skipped. With the variable
unset nothing changes. There is no registry setting, so nothing a program
in the prefix writes makes a plugin load in later processes. A plugin
must be an x86_64 (or universal) Mach-O, as the driver runs under Rosetta
2 on Apple silicon. Its constructors run on a Wine thread inside the
driver's DllMain, with the loader lock held and Cocoa not yet started: they
mustn't call into Wine or wait on the main thread, and AppKit work has to

header.why:
A program run as a helper of an app that embeds Wine shouldn't put a
Dock icon or a menu bar on screen, or take focus from the app. The Mac
Driver "ActivationPolicy" value, read the usual two ways
(HKCU\Software\Wine\Mac Driver, overridden by AppDefaults\<exe>\Mac
Driver), takes "regular" (the default, Wine's behaviour) or "accessory"
(a string, either case; any other value means regular).
The environment variable WINEMAC_ACTIVATION_POLICY, set to either,
overrides the registry, so a launcher can set it for the programs it runs
(installers during a build, say) without changing the prefix. With
"accessory", topmost (WS_EX_TOPMOST) windows also stay at the normal
window level, since the process is never active: TopmostFloatInactive is
treated as none whatever it's set to, and -adjustWindowLevels doesn't
raise them to its floor for floating windows (above the Dock, level 21),
which otherwise applies whatever TopmostFloatInactive says.
macOS also shows an accessory app's windows over another app's fullscreen
Space, even while the accessory app is inactive; a regular app's windows
aren't. Of the collection behaviours tried on a native accessory window
(default, FullScreenPrimary, Managed, MoveToActiveSpace, Transient), only
FullScreenNone kept it out. So with "accessory", -adjustFullScreenBehavior:
clears FullScreenPrimary and FullScreenAuxiliary and sets FullScreenNone.
With "accessory", the process gets NSApplicationActivationPolicyAccessory
when it first shows a window, instead of the regular policy and the Wine
menu, and the driver never asks macOS to activate it. Its windows are
still shown. Any other value, or none, changes nothing.

header.why:
Some old programs (Director projectors among them) refuse to start, or
draw wrongly, unless the screen is 8 or 16 bits, and a Mac display is
always 32. AppDefaults\<exe>\Mac Driver\ColorDepth (8, 16 or 24, as a
string or a DWORD; there is no global value) makes GetDeviceCaps(BITSPIXEL)
on a screen DC answer that in that program. Only calls through gdi32 get
it, Wine's own DLLs in the program included (user32 then picks 256-colour
icon images, comctl32 makes 8-bit image lists), as on an 8-bit Windows
screen. win32u asks NtGdiGetDeviceCaps itself and keeps the real depth, so the
bitmaps Wine makes for the screen stay 32-bit. Telling win32u too makes
compatible bitmaps 8-bit with Wine's fixed colour table, and pictures
drawn through them lose their colours. At 8 bits a program also reads the
system palette after realizing its own (Director asks for all 256
entries) to learn what its pixels will show as. Wine has no system
palette, so gdi32 notes the palette of more than 20 entries the program
last selected for the foreground into a screen DC (not a memory DC, which
Windows' system palette doesn't follow either) and GetSystemPaletteEntries
on a screen DC answers as Windows would once it was realized: the 20
static colours at either end, the palette's own entries between them.
Without the value nothing changes. The display modes Wine reports are
unchanged. A palette noted and then deleted is forgotten (the middle
entries come back black, as they do before any palette is noted).

program's input, focus, close and quit from it. A process of the same

header.uncertain:
what waiting for glFinish at each present costs a demanding
program; d3d9test drew 279 frames in 18.3 s hosted, 19.9 s on the plain

header.why:
An app that embeds Wine wants a program's windows inside its own
windows, scaled or letterboxed as it likes, and the input back, without
the program putting windows of its own on screen. The protocol is
docs/app-embedded-protocol.md, its wire format
docs/app-embedded-protocol.h (copied here as wmh_protocol.h, which is
offered under LGPL-2.1-or-later OR MIT, as hosts compile it in). With
HostWindows ("y"; HKCU\Software\Wine\Mac Driver, or per program under
AppDefaults\<exe>\Mac Driver) and WINEMAC_HOST_SERVICE naming a host's
Mach service, the driver does the handshake before Cocoa starts. If it
succeeds, each window's Cocoa functions send messages to the host instead
of making an NSWindow, window surfaces are drawn into IOSurfaces the host
is sent (up to three per window, each handed back by surface_release),
and a receive thread turns the host's input, focus, close and quit
events into the usual macdrv events. Without the variable, or if the host
doesn't answer in 10 seconds, the plain driver is used and an err: line
says why. NSApplication still runs (for the main-thread dispatch, event
queues, displays, the pasteboard and keyboard layouts), but the process
shows no window, Dock icon or menu bar of its own. The design doc said
no NSApplication; keeping it changed much less of the driver.
OpenGL (and Direct3D through wined3d, and DirectDraw wrappers that use
OpenGL) goes to the host as views: each client surface is a view of its
window, and framebuffer 0 of its drawable is remapped, in the GL functions
the driver hands out, to an FBO on an IOSurface from the view's pool;
each present finishes, sends the surface (bottom-up) and points the FBO
at a free one. Win32u, opengl32 and wined3d are unchanged. The context
is kept current with no view attached. The cursor goes to the host too:
a system cursor by its NSCursor name, an image as an IOSurface (the
first frame of an animated one), hidden; SetCursorPos and ClipCursor are
passed on, and the cursor position is the last one the host reported.
The host can ask for a window's size limits (WM_GETMINMAXINFO) and say
a resize is starting; the driver posts those as queries without waiting
and answers with window_min_max. Repeated identical messages aren't
resent.
If the host's connection fails (it goes away, or a receive fails), the
program is asked to quit.
Covered: the handshake, windows, GDI surfaces, OpenGL views, cursor,
size limits, keys, mouse, focus, close and quit; displays_get is
winemac-host-displays.

header.why:
With HostWindows (winemac-host-windows) the host shows the program's
windows, and it may show them on less than the whole screen: Second
Chance keeps them below a MacBook's notch. Until now the driver still
took its monitors from NSScreen and its current mode from

and Second Chance needed a helper injected into Wine that changed what

(displays_get) when it enumerates the displays: each monitor's rect and
work area are the host's display, the current mode's size is that
display's size (refresh rate and depth stay the real mode's), that size
is listed among the modes, and setting it changes nothing real. A screen
the host doesn't report is left out. The host's first display must be at
the protocol's origin; when it isn't, or the host doesn't answer or
answers unsupported, the driver uses the real displays. A host that
answers unsupported isn't asked again by that process; one that doesn't
answer within the call timeout (2 s) is asked again at the next
enumeration, so a host that was slow once still gets its displays used.
DISPLAYS_CHANGED from the host already reached Wine's display-change
handling, which enumerates again. Plain mode is unchanged.

program saw that monitor, work area, current mode and SM_CX/CYSCREEN,

OSXSAVE bit first don't run XGETBV under Rosetta's default CPUID, so
this matters for programs that skip that check.

header.summary: Retry write faults on pages mapped both writable and executable
header.uncertain:
when Rosetta lets such a fault through. Whether smc-rwx guards
this patch: on macOS 26.7.2 it passes without the hack firing, and its
failure on plain Wine on macOS 15 may be the wow64 mode-switch crash
that wow64cpu-rosetta-lretq works around (WineHQ bugs 60034, 60494). The
guard catches a toggle that doesn't make the page writable; if Rosetta
went on faulting a page that is writable, the write would still be
retried for ever. A plain retry-once (same address twice from one
thread) can't be used: a program that rewrites and runs the same code in
a loop (tests/regress/smc-rwx) faults at the same address and
instruction every round, legitimately.
header.why:
Under Rosetta 2 a write fault can hit a page that is mapped both
writable and executable (presumably Rosetta write-protecting a page whose
code it has translated), and Wine, which doesn't expect a write fault on
a writable page, raises an access violation. On macOS, drop and re-add
exec on the page and retry the write instead. The retry happens only if
the page is writable at the Mach level afterwards, so a page whose
protection Wine can't change doesn't fault the same write for ever.

destructor doesn't free() it. Measured on a 10.0 build (macOS 26.7.2):
%gs:0x60 is the PEB in the main thread and a new thread.

header.summary: Disable a global low-level hook that stops answering, so input keeps working
header.uncertain: CrossOver 26 no longer carries this; why isn't known.
header.why:
A global low-level keyboard or mouse hook is called by sending a
message to the thread that set it, and input waits up to 2 s for the
answer. When a hook's thread doesn't answer in time, the hook is now
removed (remove_hook()), so one stuck hook can't delay every key press and
mouse event on the desktop until Wine considers the thread hung (5 s
without reading messages). Windows 7 and later do the same: a low-level
hook that times out is removed without notice. WineHQ 11.22 still only
times out (send_hook_ll_message).

address-size prefix (fs:[disp16]) right after the thread returns from an

header.summary: Clear Mach exception ports inherited from the parent, such as a crash reporter's
header.upstream: candidate (not drafted; kept on Second Chance's list for later)
header.why:
Mach task exception ports are inherited across fork and exec. When
the program that starts Wine has a task-level crash handler (Sentry,
KSCrash), faults, bad instructions, breakpoints and software exceptions in
the Wine process go to it rather than becoming the signals Wine's
exception handling is built on, and a Windows program hangs at its first
such exception that goes to the handler. ntdll now clears every task
exception port (EXC_MASK_ALL, as Second Chance does before starting Wine)
when it sets up signal handling, except under a debugger (P_TRACED),
which uses them. It used to clear only bad access, bad instruction and
arithmetic, and the first int3 still hung under an inherited breakpoint
port (measured on 10.0 and 11.22).

header.seen_on:
macOS 26.7.2 (M1 Max): cross-process-code-write fails 3 of 3 with
the toggle turned off (an interposer hiding sysctl.proc_translated)
header.summary: Rosetta 2: make it notice code written into another process
header.uncertain:
a thread of the target that touches a toggled page (runs code
on it or reads it) while it's PAGE_NOACCESS faults. Toggling to the same
protection minus execute instead doesn't reach Rosetta in every case:
Rosetta retranslates only when the page's host protection really changes,
and with DEP off in a 32-bit process Wine keeps PROT_EXEC, so
PAGE_EXECUTE_READ to PAGE_READONLY and back changes nothing (new code
seen 0 of 10 on 11.22 and on 10.0; 10 of 10 with DEP on, and with DEP off
on PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE). Toggling to the protection plus write
(PAGE_EXECUTE_READ to PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE and back) reached Rosetta in
every case measured, with no faults while two threads ran code on the
page (10 of 10 each: i686 with DEP on and off, x86_64, both protections;
11.22 quick build, macOS 26.7.2, M1 Max, 2026-11-26), but isn't tried with
image views (PAGE_EXECUTE_WRITECOPY), views of read-only sections, which
refuse it, or a real program
header.why:
NtWriteVirtualMemory writes another process's memory with
mach_vm_write from wineserver, and Rosetta doesn't notice code changed
that way: the target keeps running its old translation. After a write
that succeeded, walk the written range region by region, and for each
region whose current protection has execute rights, change that part's
protection to PAGE_NOACCESS and back from inside the target
(NtProtectVirtualMemory on the process handle), so Rosetta retranslates.
Armadillo, the DRM in Big Fish games, writes "jmp $" (EB FE) over its
child's entry point, waits for the child to reach it, then writes the
original bytes back; without this the child spins on the stale "jmp $"
for ever and activation fails. Toggling the entry page's protection by
hand inside a stuck gmActivator child (lldb, mprotect) let it continue
as on Sikarugir 10.0_8 (2026-11-15). CrossOver's version decides from the
first region's AllocationProtect, which is PAGE_EXECUTE_WRITECOPY for
every page of an image, so a write into an image's data made the page
PAGE_NOACCESS for a moment and killed the target when another thread
touched it (a child written every 5 ms died after 4-5 writes, 12 of 12).

header.summary: Deliver WM_PAINT for composited windows straight away in one PeekMessage case
header.uncertain:
which program CrossOver wrote it for, and whether Windows behaves
this way. The flags must match exactly: PM_QS_INPUT as Windows 8+ headers
define it (with QS_TOUCH and QS_POINTER), so programs built with older
headers, or passing PM_REMOVE alone, are unaffected. None of the likely
candidates reaches the code path: Big Fish Game Manager, Iji, Icy
Tower's Inno 5.1.2 installer, and the Webmaster and Bioscopia Director
projectors made no PeekMessage call with those flags (or the pre-Windows
8 value) and had no WS_EX_COMPOSITED window (relay probe, Sikarugir
10.0_8, macOS 26.7.2, 2026-11-26); Steam's client wasn't tried.
header.why:
When a program peeks with exactly PM_REMOVE | PM_QS_INPUT |
PM_QS_POSTMESSAGE | PM_QS_PAINT | PM_QS_SENDMESSAGE and the message is
WM_PAINT for a WS_EX_COMPOSITED window, send WM_PAINT to the window straight
away and keep looking without PM_QS_PAINT, instead of returning it. If the
window procedure leaves the window invalid, a loop such as
while (PeekMessage(...)) DispatchMessage(...) otherwise gets WM_PAINT on
every call and never ends; with this, PeekMessage returns FALSE once the
queue has nothing else. Posted and sent messages arrive either way.

header.why:
With EmulateModeset on, win32u creates each window's GL client surface
"raw" and renders into a framebuffer surface (an FBO of the emulated,
virtual size) that it blits to the client surface at the monitor's real

header.summary: Skip the int 68h/41h SoftICE probes that Wine's macOS code segment provokes (Armadillo DRM)
header.uncertain:
it applies to every 32-bit program, since every one runs in
that segment under Wine on macOS, not only those that took a 9x path. An
NT program that runs int 41h or int 68h expecting the access violation
now gets nothing, with AX unchanged, which the common checks read as "no
SoftICE" (no such program known). Intel Macs use the same code segment
and should need it too; not tested on one.
header.why:
On macOS Wine runs 32-bit code in an LDT code segment (cs 0x107), not
NT's 0x23. Armadillo, the DRM in Big Fish games, tells Windows 9x from NT
by the high byte of %cs, so under Wine it takes the 9x path and probes for
the SoftICE debugger with "int 68h" (and "int 41h"). On a real 9x without
SoftICE those do nothing; here they fault. In Armadillo's child process
the fault goes to its debugger (the parent), whose debugger thread is
meanwhile in WaitForInputIdle on the child, so the launcher stalls and the
game never starts. Only in that LDT code segment, step over int 68h/41h
as 9x would.

header.summary: Keep wow64 TEBs and the PEB just under 2G, as Windows 7 does (Armadillo DRM)
header.uncertain:
why the address matters to Armadillo. Windows 7 has the TEB and
PEB just under 2G; later Windows versions place them lower (not
checked), yet Armadillo works there. Two changes that both put
them at 0x7ffdx000 fix it on Wine; the main stack stays low in both.
header.upstream:
candidate (draft in .local/bug-reports/; the placement changed
in Wine 11.18, f0bd9046, and master is unchanged, checked 2026-11-25)
header.why:
Wine 11.18 (upstream f0bd9046, "Allocate initial TEB and process
parameters in high memory on 64-bit") stopped reserving the TEB block
top-down. In wow64 that moved the 32-bit TEBs and the PEB from just under
2G to the bottom of the address space, next to the main stack. Armadillo,
the DRM in Big Fish games, then fails to unpack in its child process
("General extraction error", hidden behind the activator), so games can't
be activated. 10.0 and 11.0-11.17 put them high, as Windows 7's wow64
does. In wow64 only, reserve TEB blocks top-down below 2G again; 64-bit
processes keep upstream's placement. Big Fish's gmActivator, in a fresh
prefix, shows the error and writes no licence on macfixes 11.22 and
writes it on 10.0; its child makes the same calls on both up to the
unpack. Either moving the TEB block high or not reserving the DOS area
(both put the TEB and PEB at 0x7ffdx000) fixes it on 11.22, with the
stack still low in both.

header.summary: Rosetta 2: refuse a program's own LDT entries, as Wine 10 did, instead of hanging
header.uncertain:
measured on macOS 26.7.2 only. A program whose LDT entry is a
flat 32-bit data segment would work under Rosetta and is now refused, as

header.why:
Wine 11 implements NtSetLdtEntries for wow64 processes and passes the
entry to i386_set_ldt. Rosetta 2 can't serve 16-bit segments: for any

and programs carried on; under Rosetta, return that again. Wine's own
32-bit code and %fs selectors don't go through NtSetLdtEntries.

limit 0x323f, 16-bit data, DPL 3). A 32-bit test program setting that
descriptor spins at 100% CPU on macfixes 11.22-build3; with this patch
the call returns 0xc0000002 and the program continues.

header.summary: Don't let the main thread and a GL thread change an OpenGL context's view at once
header.uncertain:
whether any program hits the double release: the stress program
shows the overlap but never crashed, and no crash has been traced to it.
The deadlock the per-context lock avoids was found by reading, not seen.
header.upstream:
no; the code is the same in WineHQ 10.0 to master and CrossOver
26.3.0 (checked 2026-11-25).
header.why:
A WineOpenGLContext's view, latent view and update flags are changed
by the GL threads (macdrv_make_context_current, macdrv_update_opengl_context)
and, for contexts added while their view wasn't drawable, by the main thread
in the content view's viewWillDraw, which calls
macdrv_update_opengl_context. Nothing serialises the two. Both can read the
same old view or latent view and release it, and the view is then released
once too often. Give each context a recursive lock, held around those
changes. The GL thread can hold it while it waits for the main thread
(OnMainThread), so viewWillDraw only tries the lock. If it's busy, the
context stays pending and the view asks to be drawn again. The lock is
per context because a GL thread waiting in OnMainThread handles window
queries, which run the program's window procedure (WM_GETMINMAXINFO at

header.uncertain:
what a program does when a 16-bit call fails; Budapi's
functions that Webmaster uses make none. A 32-to-16 thunk can only be
called after ThunkConnect32 succeeds, which it now can't, so the thunks'

header.why:
kernel32's 16-bit thunks (LoadLibrary16, GetProcAddress16,
FreeLibrary16 and the like) are forwarded to krnl386.exe16, so a 32-bit
DLL that imports any of them makes the loader load krnl386.exe16 and run
its attach, even if it never calls one. The attach loads the 16-bit
KERNEL, which needs LDT entries for its segments. Under Rosetta 2,
NtSetLdtEntries refuses them (ntdll-rosetta-refuse-ldt-entries), krnl386

(Wine 11.22: a write to address 0xc22). The attach failed, and with it the
importing DLL. Now the attach first checks that LDT entries can be set,
and if not, succeeds without loading the 16-bit KERNEL or giving threads a
16-bit stack. A 16-bit call made anyway then fails with an error in the
log instead of a fault: loading a 16-bit module (LoadLibrary16,
LoadModule16, and ThunkConnect32, which loads the 16-bit side of a thunk)
returns 2, file not found, and a call into 16-bit code (WOWCallback16Ex,
which the 32-to-16 thunks go through) returns FALSE. Before, both faulted
in the same way as the attach. Where LDT entries work nothing changes.
On 10.0 nothing needs to come before it: its x86_64 NtSetLdtEntries always
returns STATUS_NOT_IMPLEMENTED, as ntdll-rosetta-refuse-ldt-entries makes
it under Rosetta 2 on 11.x.

header.messages:
"status block %p isn't writable; result %#x not stored" (WARN,
shown only with WINEDEBUG=warn+server)
header.programs:
Steam's updater (11.22 on macOS 15): after "Update complete,
launching Steam..." a thread holding the loader lock stored a 32-bit
status block into a reserved, uncommitted page and hung; every other
thread then waited on the loader lock, so the updated Steam never started
header.seen_on:
macOS 15.6.1 (Steam's updater, 11.22); macOS 26.7.2
(tests/regress/async-iosb-decommitted, 10.0, 11.21 and 11.22)
header.summary: Don't fault in a system APC storing an async result into a status block that isn't writable
header.uncertain:
the APC's callback can also write the program's buffer (a read's
data); that isn't covered here, and didn't fault for Steam. Wine 10.0 has
the same code; why Steam reaches it only on 11.x isn't known. That Windows
drops a status block it can't write is from how its I/O manager is
described, not measured.
header.upstream: candidate (not drafted; WineHQ master still has the bug, 2026-11-24)
header.why:
When an asynchronous read or write finishes, the APC_ASYNC_IO system
APC stores the result in the caller's IO_STATUS_BLOCK (set_async_iosb). A
thread that is running its own code gets system APCs through SIGUSR1, and
runs them on the signal stack. If the status block is no longer writable
memory, the store faults there; the fault can't be handled in a signal
handler ("nested exception on signal stack"), and the thread never
returns to its code. The status block can be freed by the program, or be
on the stack of a thread that has exited, in which case the server gives
the APC to any thread of the process. Windows ignores a status block it
can't write. Now the result is stored with
virtual_uninterrupted_write_memory, which checks the pages first, and is
dropped with a warning if they aren't writable. Information is still
written before Status, as set_async_iosb does. An ntdll.so that logged
each SIGSEGV showed Steam's updater faulting this way (11.22): a write to
a 32-bit status block's Information field in a reserved page.

header.summary: Exit a process when its wineserver is gone
header.uncertain:
macOS only (kqueue); other systems keep the old behaviour. The
cost of the watcher thread waking each time the server sends the
process a file descriptor isn't measured.
header.why:
A Wine thread only finds out that the wineserver has gone when its
next request fails (abort_thread), and the process ends with its last
Wine thread. A thread that only sleeps (a non-alertable Sleep is local),
renders, or waits in a macOS run loop makes no request, so after the
server died (killed, or crashed) such a process ran on with its windows
and open files, and an app embedding Wine couldn't tell its program had
gone. Now each process watches its socket to the server (fd_socket) with
a kqueue in a thread of its own, with every signal blocked, and exits
(status 1, "wine: the server is gone; exiting") when the server's end
closes. The server closes that socket only when it exits or has killed
the process, so nothing that should go on running is stopped. Measured
on 11.22 without it: a program whose threads only sleep, the prefix's
explorer.exe and its service processes were still running long after
wineserver -k9 (half an hour to two hours).

Wine takes a click in -[WineApplicationController handleEvent:], before

header.summary: Keep the cursor clip in step when the clipping window moves or resizes
header.uncertain:
Only the confinement handler (the default) does this; the event
tap handler (UseConfinementCursorClipping=n) clips to the screen rect and
doesn't depend on the window. If the window moves so the clip rect no

header.summary: Keep an abandoned mutex alive while its waiters are woken, so wineserver doesn't crash
header.why:
On 10.0 (WineHQ's release, without msync or esync), when a thread
exits owning a mutex whose last handle was closed while another thread
waited on it, the waiter's wait is the mutex's last reference. Abandoning
the mutex wakes the waiter, the end of its wait frees the mutex, and
wake_up() then reads the freed mutex's wait queue to go on: wineserver
crashes ("wineserver crashed, please enable coredumps") and every
program in the prefix exits with it. AddressSanitizer on 10.0's
wineserver: heap-use-after-free in wake_up (thread.c), freed by
end_wait under the same wake_up, from abandon_mutexes and kill_thread.
abandon_mutexes() now holds a reference to each mutex across
do_release(). 11.x doesn't crash (an owned mutex holds a reference
there).

patches/winehq/targeted-fixes/2077-serve.name: server-keep-abandoned-mutex-alive

origins.note:
WineHQ fixed the same use-after-free in 10.12 by having an owned
mutex hold a reference to itself (934514db, "server: Keep owned mutex
syncs alive until abandoned"), after it had split the mutex's sync
state into an object of its own. Ported to 10.0, where the mutex is
still the named object, that reference would also keep an owned
mutex's name reachable after its last handle is closed, so this fix
holds a reference only while abandon_mutexes() wakes the waiters.

header.summary: Add the flavour's name to the version string, as in "wine-<version> (macfixes)"
header.why:
Marks the build as patched, so a log or bug report shows which
flavour it came from: `wine --version` and wine_get_build_id() read
"wine-11.21 (macfixes)"; wine_get_version() still returns WineHQ's
"11.21". build/compile.sh sets WINE_VERSION_LABEL to
" (<flavour>)" for flavours that take the version-label set; the rule in
configure.ac and configure (both patched, so no autoreconf is needed)
appends it when dlls/ntdll/unix/version.c is generated. Unset, the
version string is WineHQ's. The label goes into a sed replacement and a C
string, so compile.sh refuses flavour names other than lower-case
letters, digits and hyphens.
